clue.text: What card players could be doing at a seance

definitions.text: What card players could be doing at a seance

parts.words: What card players could be doing at a seance
parts.note: card players clutch their dealt cards, while sitters round a seance table link fingers in a circle: one phrase covers both pictures

explanation.surface: A whimsical image of a card school that has wandered into a seance.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase has two senses: card players grip their dealt cards, and people at a seance sit in a ring with linked fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names linking palms with another person, and card players also grip their dealt cards.

clue.text: Cheer up the Hungarian capital with neater construction…

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its opening letter, here of the word Hungarian
construction means the letters of neater are built into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An instruction to lift the spirits of Budapest by tidying it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Hungarian capital' tempts one to think of Budapest, but it is only the first letter, H. 'construction' rearranges NEATER into EARTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To encourage someone is to lift their spirits and give them courage.

clue.text: … thus becoming more elevated

parts.note: continues the previous clue: someone who has been cheered up is lifted higher in spirits, so is raised more

explanation.surface: A continuation of the previous clue: cheered up and so raised higher.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to 1 Down: having been cheered up, one is in higher spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative adjective for something set higher or nobler, as spirits rise when cheered.

clue.text: Not in good shape

parts.note: reads as unfit or poorly, but means not having a neat, even outline

explanation.surface: A description of someone who is unfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good shape' suggests fitness, but the clue means a form that is uneven or lopsided.
explanation.definitionFit: An uneven or asymmetric outline lacks the regular form of a proper shape.

clue.text: Very loud in airy talk, they're hooked on fish

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other, the loudness marking set within the talk

parts.note: gas is empty, boastful chatter
ff (fortissimo) is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Loud empty chatter about people addicted to fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they're hooked on fish' sounds like addicts, but these are hooks that are fixed into a landed fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers use these barbed poles to haul a big catch out of the water.

clue.text: Divine spirit bringing us to prayer

parts.note: an angel is a heavenly spirit, a messenger of God

explanation.surface: A heavenly messenger leading the faithful to their devotions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catholic devotion commemorating the Incarnation, said morning, noon and evening at the sound of a bell.

clue.text: Set to 'do battle once around Reading

indicators.note: around means the letters of the word Reading are moved about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Readying for an old-time fight somewhere near the town of Reading.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading looks like the Berkshire town, but it is the anagram fodder; 'around' rearranges it. The word is archaic, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic legal and military verb meaning to vindicate a claim by combat, or to array troops for a fight.

clue.text: It doesn't become an adult

parts.note: become here means suit or befit, not turn into: the clue describes conduct unbecoming in a grown-up

explanation.surface: A remark that some trait is not what a child grows into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'become' first reads as 'grow into', but it means 'suit': infantile behaviour does not suit a grown-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Immaturity and silliness are traits that look unseemly in a grown-up.

clue.text: Has vital statistics ever in mind?

definitions.text: Has vital statistics ever in mind?

parts.words: Has vital statistics ever in mind?
parts.note: vital statistics suggests bust, waist and hip measurements, but the reading is someone always thinking about numbers

explanation.surface: A question about a person preoccupied with body measurements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vital statistics' are a person's chest, waist and hip measurements; the phrase describes someone gifted with numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone with a natural aptitude for arithmetic.

clue.text: See 8
Good enough for a city of stars, anyway

indicators.note: anyway means in any order at all, so the letters of these words are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Praise for a place like Hollywood, home of film stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a city of stars' calls up Hollywood, but its twelve letters are the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adequate meets the required standard without excelling.

clue.text: Obviously not being above board

parts.note: above board reads as honest, but board here means meals: renting out rooms without meals provided

explanation.surface: A description of some dishonest dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'above board' suggests honesty, but board here is meals: a landlord renting out rooms without meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Renting out a room or property to a tenant, as distinct from offering full board.

clue.text: Therefore look first for a performer

parts.note: so means therefore
lo is an old word for look or behold
1st, written IST, is the abbreviation for first

explanation.surface: Advice on where to look first when hunting for an entertainer.
explanation.definitionFit: A musician or singer who performs alone or takes the featured part.

clue.text: One takes it as red in archery

definitions.text: One takes it as red in archery

parts.words: One takes it as red in archery
parts.note: plays on take it as read; on an archery target the ring round the gold is coloured red

explanation.surface: A play on 'take it as read', set at an archery range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes it as red' puns on 'take it as read'. On an archery target the ring just outside the gold centre is red.
explanation.definitionFit: The ring of the target next to the bull is coloured red.

clue.text: Like melodies so romantic

definitions.note: describes what such tunes are, rather than standing in for a noun

parts.note: to like is to love, in a milder degree
songs are melodies

explanation.surface: A remark that tunes are terribly sentimental.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: 'so romantic' describes these tunes rather than naming them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballads about romance and courtship are the sentimental genre of popular music.

clue.text: Cloakroom attendant on the parish council?

definitions.text: Cloakroom attendant on the parish council?

parts.words: Cloakroom attendant on the parish council?
parts.note: the room where clergy robe is a kind of cloakroom, and the man attending it sits on the church's governing body

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about a coat-check worker serving on a local council.
explanation.walkthrough: A vestry is the room where clergy keep vestments, a cloakroom of sorts, and also a body that ran parish affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the parochial board that once managed a church's business and local affairs.

clue.text: Spiced wine the Father of Medicine made the most of

indicators.note: only most of the name is used, some of its letters being dropped

parts.note: the Greek physician Hippocrates is called the Father of Medicine

explanation.surface: The great physician enjoying a glass of mulled wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made the most of' sounds like enjoying, but it means use most of the name: drop TE from the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval cordial of wine sweetened and flavoured with spices, strained through a 'Hippocrates' sleeve' cloth bag.

clue.text: Role allowed Chanticleer's mate

parts.note: a part is a role in a play
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A part granted to the cockerel's partner in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Chanticleer is the cockerel in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale; his favourite hen is Pertelote, a name that became a general word for a hen.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional name for a hen, from the hen-wife of the rooster in medieval fable.

clue.text: Clearly nonstop progress

parts.note: progress that keeps moving without a break is plainly still happening

explanation.surface: A remark that advancement is evidently continuous.
explanation.definitionFit: Something continuing without interruption is still in progress.

clue.text: Monster of hardy constitution

indicators.note: constitution means the make-up of the word hardy, so its letters are put together afresh

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A beast with a robust physical make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constitution' looks like physical health, but it is the signal to rearrange HARDY.
explanation.definitionFit: The many-headed serpent of Greek myth slain by Heracles.

clue.text: Grip to which a shocked Lady Bracknell gave expression

definitions.text: Grip to which a shocked Lady Bracknell gave expression

parts.words: Grip to which a shocked Lady Bracknell gave expression
parts.note: grip means a small bag; in Wilde's Importance of Being Earnest Lady Bracknell is famously appalled that a baby was found in one

explanation.surface: A literary allusion to a scandalised aunt reacting to a piece of luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oscar Wilde's play, Lady Bracknell exclaims in horror on hearing that Jack was found as a baby in a lady's bag at Victoria station.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip is an old word for a travelling bag; this is a woman's small bag for carrying belongings.

clue.text: Use it to expand the muscles-and survive longer, say

definitions.text: Use it to expand the muscles-and

indicators.note: say signals that the words are to be pronounced, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: to survive longer is to die later

explanation.surface: Advice on a muscle-stretching device that also prolongs life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'die later' is pronounced like the answer. The definition is a muscle or instrument that widens an opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A muscle or device that widens or opens a passage or orifice.

clue.text: Furious finding English gar den in disarray

indicators.note: in disarray means the letters are thrown into confusion and reordered

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Anger at finding an English garden in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gar den' is split in the print; E for English stands first, and 'in disarray' rearranges GARDEN into NRAGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone livid with anger is in a rage.

clue.text: Mother gets about in a reverie

indicators.note: gets means the mother takes the other piece into herself, holding it inside

parts.note: dam is a mother, especially of an animal
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Mum wanders about lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mother' here is a mother animal rather than MA, and 'gets' means she takes the other piece inside her.
explanation.definitionFit: A daydream or state of abstraction is a waking fantasy.

clue.text: It appears right round the fireplace curled up

annotationWithheld.why: It appears right round the fireplace curled up: R + INGLE (fireplace) gives RINGLE, but no clue word clearly accounts for the final T; 'It appears' cannot be parsed honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: It appears right round the fireplace curled up

clue.text: St. Andrew's cross with the old sailor showing resentment

parts.note: an old salt is a seasoned sailor
ire is anger or resentment

explanation.surface: Scotland's flag flown by a resentful old seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: St Andrew's cross is the X-shaped cross on the Scottish flag.
explanation.definitionFit: The diagonal X-shaped cross associated with Scotland's patron saint.

clue.text: One of the gang common in America

definitions.text: One of the gang common in America

parts.words: One of the gang common in America
parts.note: the mob is the American term for an organised criminal gang, and this is one of its members

explanation.surface: A remark about a typical gang member in the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: An American term for a member of an organised criminal gang.

clue.text: Just the chap to handle Wells Fargo

definitions.text: Just the chap to handle Wells Fargo

parts.words: Just the chap to handle Wells Fargo
parts.note: Wells Fargo ran stagecoaches in the Old West, so a manager of stagecoaches would run it; the phrase also names a theatre role

explanation.surface: Picking a man to run the famous Old West coach company.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells Fargo ran stagecoach lines; the phrase also names the person running a theatre production backstage.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who runs the backstage side of a theatre production, or here, a manager of coaches.
